preamble: Retroflexion of the lateral [l] to the voiced retroflex stop [ɖ] is characteristic of the far south of the Italo-Romance area. In Sicilian, Latin geminate -ll- normally became long [ɖː] (bellus > beḍḍu 'beautiful', caballus > cavaḍḍu 'horse'); the same outcome is found in Sardinian (Nuorese cabaddu /kaˈbaɖɖu/), Southern Corsican and some Calabrian dialects. Some Sicilian dialects retain the older [lː], and a dental [dː] pronunciation is spreading. In Havana, a retroflex variety of the western Cuban Spanish assimilation of coda /l/ and /ɾ/ gives an unreleased [ɖ˺] before /t/ and /n/ (alto a[ɖ˺ʈ]o, rosal nuevo rosa[ɖ˺ɳ]uevo; Guitart 1978, 2004 and Choy López 1988, as summarized by Arias 2019), where the variety without retroflexion has [d˺t] and [nn]. In alrededor the variety without retroflexion merges /lr/ into [r], while the retroflex variety has a[ɖ˺ɽɽ]ededor, with a retroflex trill. There is no retroflexion when the next consonant is a dental stop followed by a rhotic (e[d˺t]rago 'el trago'; Guitart 1978). Word-finally Arias also reports a retroflex [ɖ] alongside [d] (alcoho[d]). In the city of Pinar del Río, the acoustic studies of Darias Concepción which do not detail phonetic contexts, give examples of postalveolar stops, alternating with other realizations, before other consonants as well (salsa sa[ɖs]a).

examples.note: The retroflex is usually long [ɖː] and is spelled ⟨ḍḍ⟩ or ⟨dd⟩; Sardinian cabaddu /kaˈbaɖɖu/ from the same Latin word shows the identical reflex.

[ɽɽ] is a retroflex trill. Arias (2019): the first element "se asimila a la articulación oclusiva del segundo elemento, pero se disimila al pasar a ser no liquido"; without retroflexion the pronunciation is a[r]ededor.
